test_text.title: What destroyed the civilisation of Easter Island?

article.title: What destroyed the civilisation of Easter Island?

items.sentence_raw: Easter Island, or Rapu Nui as it is known locally, is home to several hundred ancient human statues - the moai.
After this remote Pacific island was settled by the Polynesians, it remained isolated for centuries.
All the energy and resources that went into the moai - some of which are ten metres tall and weigh over 7,000 kilos - came from the island itself.
Yet when Dutch explorers landed in 1722, they met a Stone Age culture.
The moai were carved with stone tools, then transported for many kilometres, without the use of animals or wheels, to massive stone platforms.
The identity of the moai builders was in doubt until well into the twentieth century.
Thor Heyerdahl, the Norwegian ethnographer and adventurer, thought the statues had been created by pre-Inca peoples from Peru.
Bestselling Swiss author Erich von Daniken believed they were built by stranded extraterrestrials.
Modern science - linguistic, archaeological and genetic evidence - has definitively proved the moai builders were Polynesians, but not how they moved their creations.
items.explain: Q14: Many students get confused because the paragraph talks about different ideas about who built the moai. But the key sentence is *'Modern science... has definitively proved the moai builders were Polynesians'* — this gives an **undisputed answer** to the question of who built them. So the heading is **ii**.

items.sentence_raw: Local folklore maintains that the statues walked, while researchers have tended to assume the ancestors dragged the statues somehow, using ropes and logs.
When the Europeans arrived, Rapa Nui was grassland, with only a few scrawny trees.
In the 1970s and 1980s, though, researchers found pollen preserved in lake sediments, which proved the island had been covered in lush palm forests for thousands of years.
Only after the Polynesians arrived did those forests disappear.
US scientist Jared Diamond believes that the Rapanui people - descendants of Polynesian settlers - wrecked their own environment.
They had unfortunately settled on an extremely fragile island - dry, cool, and too remote to be properly fertilised by windblown volcanic ash.
When the islanders cleared the forests for firewood and farming, the forests didn't grow back.
items.explain: Q21: The passage says the islanders *'cleared the forests for firewood and farming'* — **'clearing land for'** something means they removed trees to use the land for that purpose. So the answer is **farming**.

items.sentence_raw: As trees became scarce and they could no longer construct wooden canoes for fishing, they ate birds.
items.explain:
Q15: The paragraph describes how the islanders lost their food sources — first they *'could no longer construct wooden canoes for fishing'*, then *'they ate birds'*, and *'soil erosion decreased their crop yields'*. All these details show their food was getting smaller and smaller. So the heading is **ix**.

Q22: The passage says they *'could no longer construct wooden canoes for fishing'* — the thing they could not build anymore was the **canoes**. So the answer is **canoes**.

Q23: The passage says that after losing their canoes, *'they ate birds'* — the birds became their new food. So the answer is **birds**.

items.sentence_raw: Soil erosion decreased their crop yields.

All these details show their food was getting smaller and smaller. So the heading is **ix**.

items.sentence_raw: Before Europeans arrived, the Rapanui had descended into civil war and cannibalism, he maintains.
The collapse of their isolated civilisation, Diamond writes, is a "worst-case scenario for what may lie ahead of us in our own future".
The moai, he thinks, accelerated the self-destruction.
items.explain: Q16: The first sentence gives the main idea: *'The moai, he thinks, accelerated the self-destruction'*. **'Accelerated'** means made something happen faster, and **'self-destruction'** means the situation became worse. So the heading is **viii**.

items.sentence_raw: Diamond interprets them as power displays by rival chieftains who, trapped on a remote little island, lacked other ways of asserting their dominance.
They competed by building ever bigger figures.
Diamond thinks they laid the moai on wooden sledges, hauled over log rails, but that required both a lot of wood and a lot of people.
items.explain: Q24: Diamond's method for moving the moai *'required both a lot of wood and a lot of people'* — the question already mentions people, so the missing thing is the other requirement. So the answer is **wood**.

items.sentence_raw: To feed the people, even more land had to be cleared.
When the wood was gone and civil war began, the islanders began toppling the moai.
By the nineteenth century none were standing.

Archaeologists Terry Hunt of the University of Hawaii and Carl Lipo of California State University agree that Easter Island lost its lush forests and that it was an 'ecological catastrophe' - but they believe the islanders themselves weren't to blame.
And the moai certainly weren't.
Archaeological excavations indicate that the Rapanui went to heroic efforts to protect the resources of their wind-lashed, infertile fields.
items.explain: Q17: The paragraph describes how the Rapanui *'built thousands of circular stone windbreaks'* and *'used broken volcanic rocks to keep the soil moist'* — these are clever, new ways to protect their land. **'Innovative'** means new and clever, so the heading is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: They built thousands of circular stone windbreaks and gardened inside them, and used broken volcanic rocks to keep the soil moist.
items.explain: Q17: The paragraph describes how the Rapanui *'built thousands of circular stone windbreaks'* and *'used broken volcanic rocks to keep the soil moist'* — these are clever, new ways to protect their land. **'Innovative'** means new and clever, so the heading is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: In short, Hunt and Lipo argue, the prehistoric Rapanui were pioneers of sustainable farming.
Hunt and Lipo contend that moai-building was an activity that helped keep the peace between islanders.
items.explain:
Q25: Hunt and Lipo believe moving the moai *'required few people and no wood'*, which is the opposite of Diamond's idea — this is a disagreement about **how the moai were transported**. They also say moai-building *'helped keep the peace'*, while Diamond saw them as causing competition and war — this is a disagreement about **the impact of the moai on Rapanui society**. So the answers are **B** and **C**.

items.sentence_raw: On that issue, Hunt and Lipo say, archaeological evidence backs up Rapanui folklore.
items.explain: Q18: The passage says *'archaeological evidence backs up Rapanui folklore'* — **'backs up'** means supports. The local belief was that the statues walked, and Hunt and Lipo's theory says they were moved upright. So the heading is **iv**.

items.sentence_raw: Recent experiments indicate that as few as 18 people could, with three strong ropes and a bit of practice, easily manoeuvre a 1,000 kg moai replica a few hundred metres.
The figures' fat bellies tilted them forward, and a D-shaped base allowed handlers to roll and rock them side to side.
Moreover, Hunt and Lipo are convinced that the settlers were not wholly responsible for the loss of the island's trees.
Archaeological finds of nuts from the extinct Easter Island palm show tiny grooves, made by the teeth of Polynesian rats.
items.explain: Q19: Hunt and Lipo argue that rats, not people, destroyed the forests — the rats *'prevented the reseeding of the slow-growing palm trees'*. This destruction was caused by animals the settlers brought, something the islanders could not control. So the heading is **vii**.

items.sentence_raw: The rats arrived along with the settlers, and in just a few years, Hunt and Lipo calculate, they would have overrun the island.
They would have prevented the reseeding of the slow-growing palm trees and thereby doomed Rapa Nui's forest, even without the settlers' campaign of deforestation.
items.explain: Q19: Hunt and Lipo argue that rats, not people, destroyed the forests — the rats *'prevented the reseeding of the slow-growing palm trees'*. This destruction was caused by animals the settlers brought, something the islanders could not control. So the heading is **vii**.

items.sentence_raw: No doubt the rats ate birds' eggs too.
Hunt and Lipo also see no evidence that Rapanui civilisation collapsed when the palm forest did.
They think its population grew rapidly and then remained more or less stable until the arrival of the Europeans, who introduced deadly diseases to which islanders had no immunity.
Then in the nineteenth century slave traders decimated the population, which shrivelled to 111 people by 1877.

Hunt and Lipo's vision, therefore, is one of an island populated by peaceful and ingenious moai builders and careful stewards of the land, rather than by reckless destroyers ruining their own environment and society.
items.explain: Q20: The paragraph directly contrasts two views: Hunt and Lipo see the islanders as *'peaceful and ingenious moai builders and careful stewards'*, while others see them as *'reckless destroyers'*. These are two completely opposite opinions. So the heading is **vi**.

items.sentence_raw: "Rather than a case of abject failure, Rapu Nui is an unlikely story of success", they claim.
Whichever is the case, there are surely some valuable lessons which the world at large can learn from the story of Rapa Nui.
